## Your turn — Exercise 1 {.smaller}

**Exercise 1.** See the local-optimum trap for yourself. Solve
$\sin(x) + \tfrac{1}{10}x^2$ from a *single* starting point at `x0 = 4`, then
compare with `best_of = 20`. Do they agree?

::: {.notes}
**Solution (presenter notes).**

```r
x <- Variable(bounds = list(-10, 10))
prob <- Problem(Minimize(sin(x) + 0.1 * x^2))

value(x) <- 4                                              # a poor starting point
one <- psolve(prob, nlp = TRUE, solver = "UNO", logger = "SILENT")

value(x) <- NULL                    # clear the fixed start so best_of can randomize
set.seed(2)
many <- psolve(prob, nlp = TRUE, solver = "UNO", logger = "SILENT", best_of = 20)
c(from_x0_4 = one, best_of_20 = many)
```
The single solve from `x0 = 4` gets **stuck in a nearby local minimum** (objective
$\approx 0.83$); the random restarts escape it and find the global one
($\approx -0.79$). This is the whole story of nonconvex optimization in one example.
:::

## Your turn — Exercise 2 {.smaller}

**Exercise 2 (⭐).** Turn on `verbose = TRUE` for one of the solves above and read
UNO's log. How is it different from the convex-solver output you saw in
@sec-gentle-intro?

::: {.notes}
**Solution (presenter notes).**

```r
psolve(prob, nlp = TRUE, solver = "UNO", verbose = TRUE)
```
You will see UNO *reformulate* the model and run a nonlinear iteration (a Newton or
SQP method), rather than the cone solver's interior-point iterations. Same
`verbose = TRUE` switch, a different engine underneath.
:::
